messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: Error While Modeling
parts:
Generally, negative variances of observed variables (Heywood cases) are a sign that the model is wrongly specified.  The program says "I found a best solution, but that best solution cannot exist in the real world". Your model fit is also not great, which also suggests that the model could be better. 

However, in your case the negative variances are not statistically significant. You might just ignore them, or you might constrain those variances to zero or a very small positive number - that should not hurt your model fit (much), but you should still convince yourself that the results are correct. 

I'm surprised that AMOS gives a different result - are the other parameter estimates (and fit indices) the same?

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Error While Modeling
parts:
Joseph,
  The answer Jeremy gave is the consensus advice and the advice that I would have given had he not gotten there first.  However, in reading the thread, it occurs to me that assuming that a unique variance equals zero has a qualitative impact on a factor model.  It basically denies the central assumption that the factor is a latent variable.  So, while the consensus advice makes sense from the perspective of frequntist hypothesis testing, it might make sense from the perspective of theoretical inference to instead fix the negative unique variances to a small positive value.  This would allow you to test a model in which the unique variances are near zero but the factors are still latent variables.  A small positive value is quantitatively more different from your negative estimates than is zero, but it is theoretically less different from your initial hypothesis about how the items work.

Keith
